receipt.answer: Checklists work when they (1) isolate killer items so one miss stops the procedure, (2) pick one method — read-do (do-list) or do-confirm (challenge-response) — and do not silently mix them, and (3) halt at named pause points at natural breaks. On this worktree, G-1 already has (1) and a do-confirm analog; it lacks named pause points and an explicit read-do versus do-confirm split.

mechanisms.name: Named pause points at natural workflow breaks
mechanisms.why_checklists_work: Haynes implements the 19-item WHO list at three critical junctures, forcing a spoken halt before anaesthesia, before incision, and before leaving the room. That is the pause-point property, not a longer to-do list.
mechanisms.section_or_figure: Intervention: 'three critical junctures in care: before anesthesia is administered, immediately before incision, and before the patient is taken out of the operating room'; Results / Table 5
mechanisms.baseline: 3733 patients before the checklist: in-hospital death 1.5%; any complication 11.0% (Table 5 totals)
mechanisms.effect_size: 3955 patients after: death 0.8% (P=0.003 vs 1.5% baseline); any complication 7.0% (P<0.001 vs 11.0% baseline)
mechanisms.strongest_caveat: Before-after, not a randomized trial. Haynes Discussion treats the mechanism as multifactorial (antibiotics, pulse oximetry, team brief). Pause points are what the intervention installed; they are not isolated as the proven causal kernel of the 1.5% to 0.8% drop. Urbach 2014 (doi:10.1056/NEJMsa1308261, Abstract) measured a mandated checklist at population scale: adjusted death 0.71% (95% CI 0.66-0.76) before vs 0.65% (0.60-0.70) after, OR 0.91 (0.80-1.03), P=0.13 — a headline 'checklists cut deaths' without that baseline is E3 and cannot promote.

mechanisms.name: Read-do (do-list) for time-critical abnormal work
mechanisms.why_checklists_work: Crisis checklists lead the operator through steps during the event (call-do-response / read-do), rather than verifying a configuration already done from memory. That is Degani's do-list method, tested as a crisis aid.
mechanisms.baseline: Without checklist (memory only): 89 of 379 critical steps missed (23%)
mechanisms.effect_size: With crisis checklists available: 24 of 371 steps missed (6%), P<0.001 vs 23% baseline; adjusted RR 0.28 (95% CI 0.18-0.42)
mechanisms.strongest_caveat: High-fidelity simulation, not live operating-room mortality. Does not show that read-do reduces deaths; it shows missed critical steps fall from 23% to 6% when the list is in hand during the crisis.

mechanisms.name: Do-confirm / challenge-response for normal work
mechanisms.cannot_promote_reason: Degani & Wiener NASA-CR-177549 §3.1.4 distinguishes challenge-response (verify after configuring from memory) from do-list (the list leads the action). No trial in the fetched CR or 1993 Human Factors paper reports an effect size against a baseline for choosing one method over the other. A headline without baseline is E3 and cannot promote this mechanism. The local G-1 live probe re-run is still measured as a do-confirm analog in the gap table.

mechanisms.name: Killer items as independently fatal, listed first
mechanisms.cannot_promote_reason: NASA-CR-177549 §3.1.6 uses the crews' phrase 'killer items' for the subset operators will still run when they shed a long list; guideline (10) says put the most critical items at the start of the task-checklist; guideline (15) says inspectors must not compromise on critical killer items. No effect size versus a baseline is reported. Cannot promote.
mechanisms.section_or_figure: NASA-CR-177549 §3.1.6 ('killer items'); Design guideline (10) critical items at the beginning; guideline (15) no compromise on critical killer items
mechanisms.strongest_caveat: Guideline, not a measured effect. Not promoted.
